level1.text: The volume of the inside of a fridge is $0.250\,\text{m}^3$. When the door has been closed for a long time, the temperature of the air in the fridge is $278\,\text{K}$ and the pressure is $1.01 \cdot 10^5\,\text{Pa}$. How many moles of air are in the fridge? Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$.

The inside volume of a basketball is $0.00710\,\text{m}^3$, and it contains $0.460\,\text{mol}$ of air. The temperature of the sports hall is $293\,\text{K}$. What is the pressure of the air inside the ball? Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. Give the answer in kilopascals.

An automatic life jacket inflates when $0.400\,\text{mol}$ of carbon dioxide is released from the cartridge of the jacket. The temperature of the gas in the jacket is $283\,\text{K}$ and the pressure is $1.05 \cdot 10^5\,\text{Pa}$. What is the volume of the gas in the jacket? Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. Give the answer in cubic metres.

On the jetty of a cottage there is a dark plastic barrel with its lid closed. The volume of the barrel is $0.200\,\text{m}^3$, and it contains $8.40\,\text{mol}$ of air. On a sunny afternoon the pressure of the air in the barrel is $1.13 \cdot 10^5\,\text{Pa}$. What is the temperature of the air in the barrel in kelvins? Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$.

The gas cylinder of a home carbonation machine contains $425\,\text{g}$ of carbon dioxide. The molar mass of carbon dioxide is $44\,\text{g/mol}$. How many moles of carbon dioxide are in the cylinder?
What does the amount of substance $n$ describe in the equation of state of an ideal gas $pV = nRT$?
level1.answer: The number of particles in moles, because one mole is always the same number of particles.

choices.text: The mass of the gas, because a heavier gas contains more matter and causes a higher pressure.
choices.feedback: Wrong: mass is obtained from the amount of substance only with the help of the molar mass, $m = nM$. There is no molar mass in the equation of state, so the type of gas does not affect the pressure.

choices.text: The density of the gas, because in a dense gas there are more particles in the same space.
choices.feedback: Wrong: density is mass divided by volume. The amount of substance is the total quantity of gas, and the volume $V$ is a quantity of its own in the equation of state.

choices.text: The number of particles in moles, because one mole is always the same number of particles.
choices.feedback: Correct: $n = N/N_\text{A}$, so the amount of substance gives the number of particles in moles. That is why the same pressure, volume and temperature mean the same amount of substance for all gases.

choices.text: The speed of the particles, because faster particles hit the wall more often.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the motion of the particles is described by the temperature $T$, which is a quantity of its own in the equation. The amount of substance tells how many particles there are.

level1.text:
A balloon is filled with helium in a room where the temperature is $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and the air pressure is $101\,\text{kPa}$. The volume of the balloon is then $2.50\,\textsf{l}$.

The balloon is taken outside, where the temperature is $-9\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and the air pressure is $98\,\text{kPa}$. The pressure of the gas in the balloon is always the same as the pressure of the surrounding air, and no gas escapes.

What is the volume of the balloon outside, in litres?

A student calculates the amount of substance of a gas when the pressure is $150\,\text{kPa}$, the volume is $0.0020\,\text{m}^3$ and the temperature is $300\,\text{K}$. The student writes

$n = \dfrac{150 \cdot 0.0020}{8.31 \cdot 300} = 1.2 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}$

The result seems small to the student, because two litres of gas surely contains more than a thousandth of a mole. What is the error in the calculation?
level1.answer: The pressure has been substituted in kilopascals instead of pascals, so the numerator is too small.

choices.text: The pressure has been substituted in kilopascals instead of pascals, so the numerator is too small.
choices.feedback: Correct: $150\,\text{kPa} = 150\,000\,\text{Pa}$. When the pressure is in pascals, the result is $0.12\,\text{mol}$, which is a thousand times larger.

choices.text: The temperature has been substituted in degrees Celsius instead of kelvins, so the denominator is too small.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the student substituted $T = 300\,\text{K}$, which is already in kelvins. If the temperature were in degrees Celsius, the result would be, on the contrary, too large.

choices.text: The molar mass of the gas is missing from the calculation, so the amount of substance cannot be calculated from the equation of state.
choices.feedback: Wrong: there is no molar mass in the equation of state. The amount of substance is obtained from the pressure, the volume and the temperature, whatever the type of gas.

choices.text: The volume has been substituted in cubic metres, although the equation of state requires it in litres.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the volume should be substituted in cubic metres when the pressure is in pascals. The student's volume $0.0020\,\text{m}^3$ is in exactly the right unit.

level1.text:
A welding gas cylinder contains $0.500\,\text{kg}$ of argon. The volume of the cylinder is $10.0\,\textsf{l}$ and the temperature of the gas is $293\,\text{K}$. Assume that argon obeys the ideal gas law, and use $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$.

Look up the molar mass of argon in the MAFY table (mafytaulukot.fi). What is the pressure of the gas in the cylinder? Give the answer in megapascals.
hints: The value is in the MAFY table *Alkuaineiden atomimassat ja moolimassat* (atomic masses and molar masses of the elements).

level2.text:
The pressure gauge of the oxygen cylinder of an ambulance is broken. The volume of the cylinder is $10.0\,\textsf{l}$, and weighing shows that the cylinder contains $2.40\,\text{kg}$ of oxygen. The temperature in the garage is $15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

What is the pressure of the oxygen in the cylinder in bars ($1\,\text{bar}$ = $100\,\text{kPa}$)?

The molar mass of oxygen is $32.0\,\text{g/mol}$. Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$ and assume that oxygen obeys the equation of state of an ideal gas.

In a chemistry storeroom there is a gas cylinder whose label is worn illegible.

A $1.00\,\textsf{l}$ glass flask emptied with a vacuum pump is filled with the gas from the cylinder, and the mass of the flask increases by $1.15\,\text{g}$. The pressure of the gas in the flask is $101\,\text{kPa}$ and the temperature is $22\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

Calculate the molar mass of the gas in grams per mole. Which gas is it, when the options are helium ($4.0\,\text{g/mol}$), nitrogen ($28\,\text{g/mol}$), oxygen ($32\,\text{g/mol}$), argon ($40\,\text{g/mol}$) and carbon dioxide ($44\,\text{g/mol}$)? Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$.

At the end of the intake stroke, the cylinder of a tractor's diesel engine contains $0.500\,\textsf{l}$ of air. The pressure of the air is $101\,\text{kPa}$ and the temperature is $30\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

At the end of the compression stroke the volume of the air is $0.0300\,\textsf{l}$ and the pressure is $4.60\,\text{MPa}$. The valves are closed, so no air can escape from the cylinder.

What is the temperature of the air at the end of compression in degrees Celsius? Diesel fuel ignites by itself at a temperature of about $250\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Does the fuel injected into the cylinder ignite?

Two identical, closed and rigid containers, each with a volume of $2.00\,\textsf{l}$, contain gas samples A and B.

When the containers are heated, their pressure is measured at different temperatures. The graph shows the measurement results.

How many moles more gas is there in container A than in container B? Read the values you need from the graph. Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$ and assume that the gases obey the equation of state of an ideal gas.

A motorist suspects that the tyre of a passenger car is leaking. The motorist measures the total pressure of the air in the tyre before driving and immediately after a long drive (example data set). The volume of the tyre is assumed to stay the same.

a) Calculate how high the pressure in the tyre would be after the drive if no air had leaked.

b) What percentage of the original amount of air in the tyre has leaked? Justify with the equation of state why measuring the pressure alone is not enough to show a leak.

The answer box takes the result of part b).

data.caption: Temperature and total pressure of the air in the tyre (example data set)

level2.text:
Students study how the volume of air depends on temperature. The air is in a syringe that is heated and whose piston moves freely. The pressure stays at atmospheric pressure, $101\,\text{kPa}$, and the amount of air stays constant. The measurement results are in the table (example data set). Draw the $(T, V)$ graph and fit a line to the points. The points are usually not exactly on a line because of measurement uncertainty.

a) Determine the slope $\Delta V / \Delta T$ of the line from two points chosen on the line, not from two measurement points.

b) Calculate from the slope the amount of substance $n$ of the air in the syringe in millimoles. Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. Justify briefly why the line should pass through the origin when the temperature is in kelvins.

The answer box takes the result of part b).

data.caption: Volume of air at constant pressure (example data set)

level2.text: The table shows the pressure of two equal amounts of gas as a function of volume (example data set). Series A and B were measured at different temperatures, and the volumes in the measurements are different. Which series was measured at the higher temperature?
level2.answer: Series B, because its product $pV$ is greater, and the temperature of the same amount of gas is proportional to it.

choices.text: Series A, because its pressure $p$ is lower, and a low pressure means faster-moving particles.
choices.feedback: Wrong: pressure also depends on the volume and the amount of substance. To compare temperatures the product $pV$ is needed, and it is smaller in series A.

choices.text: Series B, because its product $pV$ is greater, and the temperature of the same amount of gas is proportional to it.
choices.feedback: Correct: the amount of gas is the same, so $pV = nRT$ gives a greater $T$ for the series whose product $pV$ is greater. In series B the product is about $305\,\text{kPa} \cdot \textsf{l}$ and in series A about $244\,\text{kPa} \cdot \textsf{l}$.

choices.text: Series A, because its pressure falls more slowly as the volume increases, so the gas is warmer.
choices.feedback: Wrong: in both series the product $pV$ stays constant, so the pressure decreases in the same way as the volume increases, in inverse proportion. How fast the pressure decreases does not tell the temperature.

choices.text: It cannot be deduced, because the volumes of the series are different and the pressure decreases in both.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the volumes can be taken into account by calculating the product $pV$. It is directly proportional to the temperature, so the temperatures can be compared even if the volumes are of different sizes.

data.caption: Pressure and volume of the same amount of gas at two temperatures (example data set)

level2.text:
Example data: a rigid, closed $2.00\,\textsf{l}$ bottle contains $0.0800\,\text{mol}$ of air, and the pressure of the gas is $100\,\text{kPa}$. A student calculates the temperature of the gas in degrees Celsius.

Row 1: $p = 100\,000\,\text{Pa}$ and $V = 0.00200\,\text{m}^3$.

Row 2: $pV = nRT$, so $T = \dfrac{pV}{nR}$.

Row 3: $T = \dfrac{100\,000 \cdot 0.00200}{0.0800 \cdot 8.31}\,\text{K}$, that is, $T \approx 301\,\text{K}$.

Row 4: $\theta = 301 + 273 = 574\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

Which row is wrong? If there is no error in the calculation, choose the last option.
level2.answer: Row 4: converting kelvins to degrees Celsius

choices.text: Row 1: the conversions of pressure and volume
choices.feedback: Row 1 is correct: $100\,\text{kPa} = 100\,000\,\text{Pa}$ and $2.00\,\textsf{l} = 2.00\,\text{dm}^3 = 0.00200\,\text{m}^3$. If you think this row is wrong, you are mixing up the litre and the cubic metre (a cubic metre contains $1000\,\textsf{l}$).

choices.text: Row 2: solving the equation of state
choices.feedback: Row 2 is correct: when the equation $pV = nRT$ is divided on both sides by the product $nR$, the temperature becomes $T = pV / (nR)$. If you think this row is wrong, you think the temperature belongs in the numerator.

Row 3 is correct: the numerator is $200\,\text{J}$, the denominator is $0.0800 \cdot 8.31 = 0.665$ and the quotient is $301\,\text{K}$. The result is already in kelvins, because the unit of $R$ contains the kelvin. If you think this row is wrong, you think the result would already be in degrees Celsius.

choices.text: Row 4: converting kelvins to degrees Celsius
choices.feedback: Correct, this row is wrong: the Celsius temperature is obtained from the kelvin temperature by subtracting $273$, not by adding. The correct value is $\theta = 301 - 273 = 28\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The result $574\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ would already be a sign of an error, because the bottle contains room-temperature air.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation
choices.feedback: There is an error in row 4. Rows 1 to 3 are correct and $T \approx 301\,\text{K}$, but in degrees Celsius that is $301 - 273 = 28\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Adding would give $574\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, which does not fit a closed bottle.

level2.text:
The graph shows the pressure of the gas in two identical, closed, rigid vessels, A and B, as a function of temperature when the vessels are heated. Each vessel has a volume of $2.00\,\textsf{l}$.

How many times as much gas is there in vessel A as in vessel B? Read the values you need from the graph and reason from the ratio of the slopes of the lines. Assume that the gases obey the ideal gas law.

level3.text:
At rest, a person breathes into the lungs with one inhalation air that takes up a volume of $0.55\,\textsf{l}$ at a temperature of $37\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The pressure of the air in the lungs is $101\,\text{kPa}$.

How many molecules are in one breath? The Avogadro constant is $6.022 \cdot 10^{23}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{mol}}$ and $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. Give the answer in the form $a \cdot 10^{22}$. Justify why the calculation does not need information about which gases the air consists of.

In new windows the space between the panes is often filled with argon, because argon conducts heat worse than air.

The panes of an insulating glass unit are $1.20\,\text{m}$ × $1.00\,\text{m}$. According to the manufacturer, an argon filling makes the unit $6.0\,\text{g}$ heavier than an air filling when the gap is filled at a pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$ and a temperature of $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

How thick is the layer of gas between the panes? The molar mass of argon is $40\,\text{g/mol}$ and that of air is $29\,\text{g/mol}$, and $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. Give the answer in millimetres.

The compressed air tank of a car workshop's compressor has a volume of $200.0\,\textsf{l}$. In the evening the pressure gauge of the tank shows $10.0\,\text{bar}$, but in the morning only $7.0\,\text{bar}$, because air leaks from a joint.

The gauge shows gauge pressure, that is, how much greater the pressure in the tank is than atmospheric pressure ($1\,\text{bar}$ = $100\,\text{kPa}$). The temperature of the workshop is $18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ the whole time.

How many kilograms of air leaked from the tank during the night? The molar mass of air is $29\,\text{g/mol}$, and $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. Justify why in this calculation the readings of the gauge can be used without adding atmospheric pressure to them.

At a party, balloons are filled from a helium cylinder whose volume is $20.0\,\textsf{l}$. The cylinder was first in a cold storeroom and was then used indoors in two stages. The table shows the total pressure indicated by the pressure gauge in bars ($1\,\text{bar} = 100\,\text{kPa}$) at three moments (example data set). The temperature of the gas in the cylinder is always the same as that of the surroundings, and the cylinder does not leak. Treat the helium as an ideal gas and use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$. The amount of helium that goes into one filled balloon is such that the balloon takes up a volume of $5.0\,\textsf{l}$ at atmospheric pressure $101\,\text{kPa}$ and temperature $21.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

a) Calculate the amount of substance of helium in the cylinder at moments 1, 2 and 3.

b) Calculate the mass of helium used between moments 1 and 3. The molar mass is $M = 4.0\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{mol}}$. Explain why the amount used cannot be calculated directly from the difference of the pressures.

c) How many balloons were filled with the helium used? How many more balloons can be obtained from the cylinder when it is used until the pressure has fallen to atmospheric pressure $101\,\text{kPa}$?

The answer box takes the mass of part b).

data.caption: Temperature and total pressure of the helium cylinder (example data set)

level3.text:
A weather balloon is filled with helium at ground level, and its volume is then $2.50\,\text{m}^3$. The table shows the pressure and temperature of the atmosphere at different heights (ICAO standard atmosphere, rounded). Assume that the pressure and temperature of the gas in the balloon are always the same as those of the surrounding air, that no gas escapes and that the balloon rises. Use the value $R = 8.31\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}}$.

a) Calculate the amount of substance of helium in the balloon at ground level.

b) Calculate the volume of the balloon at a height of $10\,\text{km}$.

c) The envelope of the balloon withstands a volume of at most $12.0\,\text{m}^3$. Calculate the volume at a height of $15\,\text{km}$ and estimate up to what height the balloon withstands: assume the volume is linear with respect to height between the heights $10\,\text{km}$ and $15\,\text{km}$. Explain why the volume increases even though the gas cools.

The answer box takes the volume of part b).
